questions.question: Describe the Earth's rotation, revolution and tilt, and explain why the Southern and Northern Hemispheres have opposite seasons.
questions.expected_answer: The Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours (day and night) and revolves around the Sun once every 365¼ days (a year). Its axis is tilted at 23,5° and always points in the same direction in space. So as the Earth orbits, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun for part of the year (around December) while the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away, and the reverse happens around June; therefore the hemispheres have opposite seasons.

questions.question: Explain how the tilt of the Earth changes the intensity of solar energy and causes summer and winter, and describe a torch demonstration.
questions.expected_answer: When a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun is high and its rays strike almost straight down, concentrating energy on a small area, so intensity is high: summer. When tilted away, the Sun is low and rays strike at a slant, spreading the same energy over a larger area (and through more atmosphere), so intensity is lower: winter. Demonstration: shine a torch straight down on paper (small, bright spot), then tilt it (larger, dimmer patch): the same energy spread over a bigger area.

questions.question: Explain why days are longer in summer than in winter in South Africa and why day length changes more in Cape Town than near the equator.
questions.expected_answer: In summer, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so places spend more than half of each rotation in sunlight (longest day about 21 December); in winter, tilted away, they spend less than half (shortest day about 21 June); at the equinoxes day and night are about equal. Because of the tilt, the further a place is from the equator, the greater the difference: Cape Town (further south) has longer summer days and shorter winter days than Pretoria, while the equator has about 12 hours all year.
